newsitem.title: CANADA: Zaire military force may not be needed - Canada.
newsitem.headline: Zaire military force may not be needed - Canada.

text.p: The planned military force in Central Africa could be scaled back to simple humanitarian relief units if conditions there continue to improve, Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young said on Monday.
But he said hundreds of thousands of refugees remained in Zaire, and Canada was willing to fight to open aid corridors if necessary and the Zairean government gave its approval.

"If we get the results hoped for, and people can return to their home countries, and humanitarian organisations can do their work without being in danger, then the mission becomes unnecessary," Young told reporters.
"No one wants to go to Zaire or Rwanda for Christmas."
He said the Canadian military's Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART), for example, might be needed to provide humanitarian care and hospital and medical aid.
"It could be decreased to just include the DART component," Young said.

The U.N. Security Council on Friday authorised an international force to help refugees return and facilitate aid deliveries but some -- including Washington -- have begun to have misgivings over whether it is necessary.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien said 400,000 refugees had already returned home and another 150,000 were likely to do so in the next few days.
Canada's position had so far been that it would be an error to hesitate now, and both Young and Chretien expressed the belief that force could still be necessary.

"We will do everything that is necessary to complete the work. We believe troops are needed, but we will be happy if there is no need," said Chretien, who staked his prestige on personally assembling the international force.
Young told Parliament: "Surely we can all agree that it is too early to say the crisis is over."
He said the multinational force would only go to countries that agreed to its presence, adding that Rwanda had made it clear over the past few days that it was not welcome.
"This is not an invasion force. We're not going anywhere where we're not wanted," he said, noting that this applied only to recognised governments and not to rebel forces.

When a reporter pointed out the force might have to fight Tutsi rebels to open up aid corridors in eastern Zaire, he answered: "We knew that. We're prepared to confront anybody that would restrict the distribution of humanitarian aid."
But he said he had no indication the rebels were preparing to confront the force.

Britain, France, Italy and the United States are among the countries that have agreed at least conditionally to join the force, but strategists everywhere are scrambling to decide exactly how it should be deployed.

Canada has sent about 200 soldiers on reconnaissance but is waiting to send the bulk of its planned 1,500-strong force to the region until it makes a proper assessment of the quickly changing situation.

The head of the overall force, Canada's Lt. Gen Maurice Baril, left Ottawa on Sunday night for Rwanda to make a personal assessment and also to make representations to the Rwanda government, a spokesman said.
He will head to Stuttgart, Germany, for a meeting on Thursday with representatives of participating countries.
Chretien's nephew Raymond Chretien is the U.N. troubleshooter for the crisis and talked with the prime minister on Sunday night.
"In talking with Ambassador Chretien, he told me that U.N. intervention was still needed," the prime minister said.

International Cooperation Minister Don Boudria announced he was convening a meeting of major aid donors in Brussels or Geneva next Saturday or Monday to help returning refugees resettle in their home countries. Canada itself is giving $15 million Canadian ($11.3 million) in refugee aid.
